parts.label: (a)
parts.part_stem: A spherical oil drop has a radius of $1.2 \times 10^{-6} \text{m}$. The density of the oil is $940 \text{kg m}^{-3}$.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Show that the mass of the oil drop is $6.8 \times 10^{-15} \text{kg}$.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: The oil drop is charged. Explain why it is impossible for the magnitude of the charge to be $8.0 \times 10^{-20} \text{C}$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
The charged oil drop in (a) is in a vacuum between two horizontal metal plates, as illustrated in Fig. 4.1.

{{figure:figure_4_1}}

Fig. 4.1

The plates are separated by a distance of $8.0 \text{mm}$. The electric field between the plates is uniform and has a field strength of $2.1 \times 10^{5} \text{V m}^{-1}$.

The oil drop moves vertically downwards with a constant speed.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Calculate the potential difference $V$ between the plates.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Explain how the motion of the oil drop shows that it is in equilibrium.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Determine the charge on the oil drop.

parts.label: (c)
parts.part_stem: The magnitude of the potential difference between the plates in (b) is decreased.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: Explain why the oil drop accelerates downwards.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Describe the change to the pattern of the field lines (lines of force) representing the uniform electric field as the potential difference decreases.

parts.label: (d)
parts.part_stem:
Two types of force, X and Y, can act on an oil drop when it is in air, but cannot act on an oil drop when it is in a vacuum. Force X can act on an oil drop when it is stationary or when it is moving. Force Y can only act on an oil drop when it is moving.
